Edmund. The bastard son of the Earl of Gloucester. He is a schemer who exploits his illegitimate status as an excuse for ruthlessness. He pits his legitimate elder brother Edgar against their father and seduces both of King Lear's cruel daughters. He embodies the theme of nature versus legitimacy. Though he calls himself nature's bastard child, as opposed to society's, his actions are purely calculated manipulation.

Edmund opens the play with a soliloquy declaring his resentment. He is the bastard son of Gloucester, born outside marriage, and thus barred from inheritance by legitimate succession. He frames his villainy as a response to social injustice. He says, "Why bastard? Wherefore base?... I grow; I prosper." Yet his actions suggest his villainy is less born of necessity than of naked ambition. He is intelligent and articulate, capable of advancement through merit, but chooses manipulation instead.

Edmund forges a letter from his brother Edgar, suggesting Edgar is plotting to kill their father and seize the earldom. He then confronts Edgar with the letter and, when Edgar flees in panic, Edmund helps his father hunt Edgar down. Edgar goes mad and disguises himself as Poor Tom. Edmund sends his father to Lear on the heath, where Gloucester is captured and blinded. Edmund benefits by having his father's lands forfeit to the crown.

Edmund seduces both Goneril and Regan, King Lear's cruel elder daughters, promising marriage to whichever gains power first. When Goneril poisons Regan, who loves Edmund, Goneril stabs herself. Edmund is now the sole obstacle to his succession. Yet both daughters' affection for him leads to mutual destruction. This suggests that Edmund's charm, like Iago's or Richard III's, masks an emptiness. He uses love as a tool.

Edmund is made Earl of Gloucester and temporarily rules. His ascent is meteoric, unchecked by conscience or fear. Edgar, still disguised as Poor Tom, defeats Edmund in single combat and reveals himself. Edmund, mortally wounded, finally confesses his crimes. Edmund even orders the death of Lear and Cordelia before dying, but his order is too late. Cordelia is already hanged.

Edmund invokes nature, calling himself nature's bastard. He claims that nature, not law, should rule, that the strongest should govern. Yet the play refutes him. Nature in the play is represented by Cordelia's love and Edgar's endurance, not by Edmund's cunning. His illegitimacy is the occasion for his ambition but not its justification.
